document.title: Protest of Northern Virginia Electric Cooperative, Inc. to the PJM Reliability Backstop Procurement Proposal

pages.text:
UNITED STATES OF AMERICA 
BEFORE THE 
FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION 
 
 
) 
 
PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. 
) 
Docket No. ER26-3380-000 
 
) 
 
 
PROTEST OF NORTHERN VIRGINIA ELECTRIC COOPERATIVE, INC. 
Pursuant to Rule 211 of the Rules of Practice and Procedure of the Federal Energy 
Regulatory Commission (“FERC” or the “Commission”),1 Northern Virginia Electric 
Cooperative, Inc. (“NOVEC”) respectfully submits this protest to aspects of the July 31, 2026, 
filing by PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. (“PJM”) to revise its Open Access Transmission Tariff 
(“Tariff”) and Reliability Assurance Agreement Among Load Serving Entities (“RAA”) to 
establish the Reliability Backstop Procurement (“RBP”).2 For the reasons set forth herein, the 
Commission should reject the RBP as unjust and unreasonable. If the Commission does not 
reject the RBP, it should require revisions on compliance to eliminate or substantially reduce the 
nearly $2 billion collateral requirement that the RBP Proposal would impose on NOVEC, and to 
eliminate the resulting subsidization of the PJM capacity market by NOVEC and a relatively 
small number of the other Load Serving Entities (“LSEs”) that would be primarily responsible 
for providing financial security for the contracts that PJM would enter into with RBP Resources. 
I. 
INTRODUCTION 
NOVEC recognizes the importance of bringing online more new capacity quickly to 
ensure system reliability and the fair assignment of associated costs. Even before the recent 
 
1 18 C.F.R. § 385.211. NOVEC filed a doc-less motion to intervene in this proceeding on August 10, 2026. NOVEC, 
(doc-less) Motion to Intervene, Docket No. ER26-3380-000 (Aug 10, 2026) (Accession No. 20260810-5101). 
2 PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., Reliability Backstop Procurement, Docket No. ER26-3380-000 (July 31, 2026) 
(Accession No. 20260731-5214) (“RBP Proposal”).

2 
 
exponential nationwide expansion of data centers and other large loads, significant numbers of 
data centers had already been locating in NOVEC’s service territory.  
NOVEC has a longstanding practice of taking steps to appropriately assign costs to large-
load customers. NOVEC developed and received state regulatory approval for, and then began 
utilizing, a data-center-specific rate class that has been in place since the 1990’s. Additionally, 
NOVEC has directly assigned more than $1.7 billion in costs directly to data-center customers to 
help ensure they pay upfront for their dedicated substations and other infrastructure. NOVEC is 
also concerned about supply-demand imbalances and the resulting cost increases impacting 
customers large and small throughout the region. 
As a result, NOVEC was encouraged by, and participated in, the PJM stakeholder process 
that utilized PJM’s Critical Issue Fast Path (“CIFP”) to address the issue of large-load additions. 
That stakeholder process successfully culminated in a coalition proposal that received more than 
two-thirds member endorsement in a sector-weighted vote. That consensus proposal “would have 
created greater stability and certainty while shielding homes and businesses from bearing the 
costs of serving large loads.”3 The coalition proposal was a bottom-up structure that relied on a 
voluntary subscription model to maintain LSEs’ authority to negotiate with large-load customers 
and only take on obligations for which it had signed contracts or otherwise secured a pathway for 
directly assigning the resulting costs to the data center causing the costs. Despite the strong 
stakeholder support, PJM rejected the consensus proposal and instead filed its RBP Proposal, a 
top-down approach that is fundamentally flawed and was not fully vetted through the stakeholder 
process. Notably, the details and full implications of the mandatory credit and collateral 
requirements were never explained. 
 
3 East Kentucky Power Cooperative, Letter of EKPC President and CEO Don Mosier, Docket No. ER26-3380-000, 
at 2 (filed Aug. 11, 2026) (Accession No. 20260811-4003) (“EKPC Letter”).

3 
 
The as-filed RBP Proposal is not just and reasonable. The accelerated schedule prevents 
the RBP from achieving the aims of mutually agreed-upon cost-causation principles. The cost 
allocation of the RBP violates the Commission’s cost-causation principle because it does not 
recognize that neither load growth of large-load customers, nor load growth in general, are the 
sole cause of the capacity shortfall. PJM’s proposal is also not just or reasonable because it 
unreasonably causes entities like NOVEC to secure and subsidize the capacity market as RBP 
buyers. Although the RBP allows RBP buyers to offset their obligations, the time allotted to do 
so is unreasonably short and the RBP requires that customers procure more MWs than they 
would otherwise be responsible for, design choices that should be rejected. Having put this 
burden on NOVEC and other RBP buyers, PJM is also proposing to impose collateral 
requirements on them that are excessive, onerous, and not commensurate with the actual RBP 
Charges that need to be collateralized. 
The Commission should reject the filing as unjust and unreasonable. If the Commission 
does not reject the filing, it should accept PJM’s invitation4 to require changes to the RBP to 
rectify the flaws discussed below, including extending the effective date to allow for the RBP to 
have a chance of success, revising the cost-allocation structure to recognize the benefits derived 
from RBP Resources by non-RBP buyers, adjusting the amount of MWs needed to offset RBP 
cost responsibility, requiring additional paths to mitigation, and reducing the collateral 
requirements as discussed below. At a minimum, the Commission should issue a deficiency 
letter and require PJM to better explain both its rejection of the coalition proposal and clarify 
PJM’s as-filed RBP design.  
 
4 RBP Proposal at 3 (“…PJM provides notice that it consents to the Commission’s exercise of authority to modify 
and/or sever any element of the proposed Tariff and RAA language to the extent necessary and permitted under 
section 205 of the FPA and NRG Power Marketing, LLC v. FERC, where such modification and/or severance is 
consistent with PJM’s overarching objectives in this filing.”) (internal citation omitted).

4 
 
II. 
PROTEST 
A. 
There is a material mismatch in the timing required by PJM’s proposed RBP 
obligation and the decisions of state regulators on allocation process requirements 
as PJM laid them out prior to the auction.  
Recognizing that the justness and reasonableness of the RBP hinges on the ability of the 
LSEs to directly assign the RBP costs imposed on them to large loads that the LSEs serve, PJM 
states that the success of the RBP relies on state participation to “refine, for purposes of cost 
allocation, which retail loads — including which ‘large loads,’ as each state defines such loads 
— should be allocated the costs of resources procured through the RBP.”5 The success, then, of 
the RBP relies on the coordination of a multidimensional amalgam of state regulatory 
commissions, legislatures, governors, local governments, and utilities across thirteen states and 
the District of Columbia. Notwithstanding that Herculean challenge, PJM plans for the 
procurement phase of the RBP to conclude less than six weeks from today’s comment date 
(specifically, within three weeks of September 30, 2026).6 In principle, NOVEC supports PJM’s 
efforts to quickly address its lack of capacity and the allocation of costs, as appropriate, directly 
to large loads but is concerned that the pace of the RBP process as PJM has proposed it will not 
afford NOVEC and others the necessary time for either RBP-obligation mitigation or completion 
of necessary regulatory proceedings to assign costs fairly and accurately to the cost-causing 
customers, to develop customer-level allocation rules, to make necessary modifications to billing 
and settlement processes, to address phased, delayed, reduced, or canceled load, and to 
implement appropriate audit and control procedures for substantial obligations lasting up to 15 
 
5 RBP Proposal at 11 (citing Statement of Principles Regarding PJM, National Energy Dominance Council, at 2 
(Jan. 16, 2026), https://www.energy.gov/documents/statement-principles-regarding-pjm (“NEDC/PJM Governors’ 
Principles”)). 
6 RBP Proposal at 3, n.5 (“To the extent the RBP framework is accepted by September 29, 2026, and absent 
significant revisions or developments, PJM intends to open the procurement window on September 30, 2026.”); id., 
Attachment A at § 18.4 (“The Reliability Backstop Procurement offer submission window for RBP Sell Offers shall 
open for three weeks in 2026.”).

5 
 
years. NOVEC is a prime example of this conundrum because its nature, as a not-for-profit 
electric cooperative, is to set up allocations before assuming obligations, but PJM is mandating 
that it assume a large obligation that it has no way to opt out of. 
 
PJM’s timeline raises additional concerns that adversely affect the market. The success of 
the RBP depends on generators offering in sufficient quantities and at competitive prices. With 
only three weeks to make informed decisions based on the final, effective version of the RBP, 
some participants may not be able to prepare offers in time to participate. Indeed, PJM has 
requested FERC approval by September 29 so it can begin the RBP auction on September 30, 
which means that participants are expected to make decisions with impacts that last the better 
part of two decades in a span of a few weeks and without knowing what the actual rules or 
approved state regulator allocations will be. The companies with the wherewithal to prepare 
offers on an expedited basis and accept the uncertainty risk are likely to be staffed sufficiently to 
gamble on whatever the RBP might turn out to be without detracting from their established 
sources of revenue and have significant market share of PJM’s existing generation. From the 
customer’s perspective, there is a risk that a paucity of true competition will result in much of the 
RBP Resources receiving guaranteed payments at the cap of $555/MW-day when, if more time 
were afforded, more participants might think through ways to offer at lower rates and still be 
profitable. Not many developers will have proposed generation sitting on the shelf ready to 
deploy into the RBP auction within such a short window. PJM’s expedited process thus risks 
unnecessarily increasing costs on the customers who will be supporting RBP Resources and 
undermines the purpose of the RBP. 
 
The expedited process also effectively forecloses NOVEC’s ability to procure Qualifying 
RBP Offset UCAP MW. As PJM explains in the transmittal letter, Qualifying RBP Offset UCAP

6 
 
MW “is new capacity voluntarily brought on to the PJM system by new load… [and] [w]here 
Electric Distributors…report Qualifying RBP Offset UCAP MW to PJM with the requisite 
supporting evidence, PJM may reduce the region-wide Initial RBP Target by the quantity of 
Qualifying RBP Offset UCAP MW, where appropriate.”7 In addition to reducing the region-wide 
RBP Target, “the pro-rata allocation of RBP UCAP MW to each Electric Distributor’s zone/area, 
and the Final RBP Target, will be further adjusted to reflect reductions for Qualifying RBP 
Offset UCAP MW and UCAP MW representing successfully supported opt-outs from RBP in 
each zone/area.”8 Thus, RBP buyers can benefit in two ways from Qualifying Offset UCAP 
MW: by a reduction to the Initial Load Adjustment MW, and by reducing the Final RBP Target, 
thus reducing the pro-rata share of RBP UCAP MW from that Final RBP Target allocated to 
each Electric Distributor’s zone.  
 
The ability to procure Qualifying RBP Offset UCAP MW is important to managing RBP 
costs for all RBP buyers, but particularly for NOVEC given the size of its obligation and the 
need to address the appropriate allocation and recovery of these new and substantial RBP costs 
from the cost-causing data centers. Despite that importance, RBP buyers have only the imminent 
and brief RBP bid-submission window in which to procure new generation.9 Just as supply-side 
participants are likely to encounter difficulties preparing offers for the RBP, NOVEC and other 
buyers will experience difficulty securing new generation by the third week of October. PJM’s 
proposed schedule provides RBP buyers an exceptionally limited period to identify and procure 
qualifying capacity. The result is an offset mechanism that may exist under the Tariff but cannot 
reasonably be utilized at the scale required. 
 
7 RBP Proposal at 35.  
8 Id., Attachment C, Affidavit of Ms. Danielle Croop at P 44 (“Croop Affidavit”).  
9 See RBP Proposal, Attachment A at § 18.2(c).

7 
 
NOVEC in particular is prejudiced because the Initial Load Adjustment MW that it 
would need to offset to eliminate its obligation in the RBP auction is so high (1,619.2 MW) that 
NOVEC is unlikely to be able to secure bilateral contracts with new generators for anything 
approaching that amount. The only other Electric Distributor who exceeds NOVEC’s initial 
allocation is in a retail-choice state where the LSEs it serves take on the obligation.10 As a rural, 
not-for-profit cooperative and a transmission-dependent distribution utility, NOVEC faces a 
procurement challenge that is unusual both in magnitude and structure. A prudent procurement 
of more than 1,600 MW cannot reasonably be completed within the period PJM proposes. A 
procurement of this magnitude would likely require multiple counterparties and transactions, 
each involving counterparty and credit diligence, commercial and risk analysis, contract 
negotiations, internal approvals, and potentially regulatory review. A conventional physical 
bilateral capacity transaction may require approximately two to four months once qualifying 
capacity has been identified, while more complex structured transactions, including power 
purchase agreements or tolling arrangements, may require four to twelve months or more to 
negotiate. PJM’s proposed schedule does not provide a commercially reasonable opportunity to 
undertake those activities, particularly for an Electric Distributor seeking capacity on the scale 
required here. 
The compressed procurement period is especially problematic because the universe of 
resources capable of qualifying as RBP offsets is itself constrained. The applicable qualification 
window limits the capacity that can serve as an offset, and PJM’s schedule provides no realistic 
opportunity to develop new generation specifically for that purpose. RBP buyers therefore are 
not entering an unrestricted capacity market with sufficient time to develop alternatives. They are 
 
10 RBP Proposal, Attachment C, Croop Affidavit at P 46.

8 
 
competing within a limited pool of qualifying resources under an unusually compressed 
deadline. 
The consequences of the compressed schedule extend beyond NOVEC. It is worth noting 
that NOVEC will not be the only Electric Distributor harmed by the constraints on NOVEC’s 
ability to assess and obtain Qualifying RBP Offset UCAP MW. In her affidavit, Ms. Croop 
walks through an example that shows how one Electric Distributor obtaining Qualifying RBP 
Offset UCAP MW reduces the final allocation of RBP UCAP MW for all RBP buyers.11 That is, 
when one RBP buyers procures some Qualifying RBP Offset UCAP MW, that act also reduces 
the final amount of RBP MW allocated to other RBP buyers as well.12 Thus, an Electric 
Distributor’s ability to obtain qualifying offsets affects the residual RBP allocation borne by 
other RBP buyers. PJM’s compressed timetable therefore does not merely impair an individual 
participant’s opportunity to mitigate its own costs. It can affect the ultimate allocation of RBP 
obligations across multiple participants.  
NOVEC is also concerned that, given the limited timeframe to choose between 
participating in the RBP auction or signing a bilateral contract, the compressed schedule and 
limited pool of qualifying resources may materially disadvantage RBP buyers in bilateral 
negotiations. Potential counterparties will know that RBP buyers face a fixed and imminent 
deadline to obtain qualifying capacity and that the alternative is exposure to an RBP allocation. 
Those circumstances reduce the ability of RBP buyers to solicit competing offers, develop 
alternative transaction structures, and negotiate from a commercially reasonable position, 
 
11 Id. PP 47-50. 
12 This is because, per the example in Croop’s affidavit, when an Electric Distributor procures generation to be 
Qualifying RBP Offset UCAP MW, it reduces both the MW load adjustment column and the Final Allocation of 
RBP UCAP MW column such that all Electric Distributor areas are allocated fewer RBP MWs. In Croop’s example, 
ODEC procuring 130 MW entitles them to 122.2 MW, but also reduces (in combination with REC’s 673.8 MW) 
NOVEC’s allocation to 1,271.6 MW from 1,302.6 MW. See id., Attachment C, Croop Affidavit at PP 47-50.

9 
 
potentially resulting in higher bilateral prices or less favorable contractual terms. PJM cannot 
reasonably rely on Qualifying RBP Offset UCAP MW as a meaningful mechanism for 
mitigating RBP obligations while establishing a schedule that prevents affected Electric 
Distributors from having a commercially reasonable opportunity to use that mechanism. The 
problem is particularly acute where, as here, PJM proposes to impose substantial long-term 
financial obligations based, in part, on whether an Electric Distributor succeeds in procuring 
qualifying offsets during this abbreviated period.  
The Commission should therefore reject PJM’s proposed implementation schedule or 
require PJM to provide RBP buyers sufficient time to conduct a commercially reasonable 
procurement of Qualifying RBP Offset UCAP MW before their final RBP obligations are 
established. At a minimum, the schedule should provide no less than four months for 
conventional bilateral capacity transactions after the universe of qualifying resources and 
applicable offset requirements are sufficiently known, with additional time where structured 
transactions are necessary. Without such an opportunity, the offset mechanism does not provide 
a meaningful means of mitigating RBP exposure, and PJM’s resulting allocation may reflect the 
constraints of its accelerated implementation schedule rather than the amount of capacity RBP 
buyers reasonably could procure.  
B. 
The RBP violates the Commission’s cost-causation principle because it does not 
recognize the structural causes of the capacity shortfall beyond load growth and 
improperly assigns all RBP costs based only on projected load growth of large-load 
customers. 
 
Section 205 requires rates to be just and reasonable.13 That standard incorporates “a ‘cost-
causation principle’—the rates charged for electricity should reflect the costs of providing it.”14 
 
13 16 U.S.C. § 824d(a).  
14 Old Dominion Elec. Coop. v. FERC, 898 F.3d 1254, 1255 (D.C. Cir. 2018).

10 
 
The cost-causation principle “add[s] flesh to the[] bare statutory bones” of the just and 
reasonable standard.15 But while cost allocation is not a matter for the “slide-rule”16 and does not 
require “exacting precision,”17 the cost-causation principle does require the Commission to have 
“an articulable and plausible reason” to believe that the benefits are roughly commensurate with 
the costs.18 A rate that assigns all the costs to a cause only partly responsible for the costs does 
not satisfy the cost-causation principle because as a “kind of equity,” the principle matches 
burden with benefit.19 
 
The RBP violates the Commission’s cost-causation principle because it assigns the costs 
of the RBP Charge and the collateral requirements to one cause without recognition of other 
significant causes of the capacity shortfall, and because it results in an improper subsidy of 
PJM’s Reliability Pricing Model (“RPM”) auction by RBP buyers for the benefit of other Market 
Participants that are not RBP buyers. 
 
The RBP process is a one-time mechanism designed to address resource-adequacy 
challenges arising from the capacity shortfall that occurred in the 2028/2029 Base Residual 
Auction (“BRA”).20 Ms. Croop explains that the “RBP will function as a safety net to address the 
shortfall MW from the 2028/2029 BRA that has not been addressed by new load bringing their 
own new capacity through bilateral agreements or otherwise.”21  
The RBP attributes the shortfall to load growth.22 PJM argues that, despite the addition of 
1,294.4 MW ICAP between the 2027/2028 and 2028/2029 BRA, the shortfall has grown.23 
 
15 K N Energy, Inc. v. FERC, 968 F.2d 1295, 1300 (D.C. Cir. 1992).  
16 United Distribution Cos. v. FERC, 88 F.3d 1105, 1167 (D.C. Cir. 1996). 
17 Coalition of MISO Transmission Customers v. FERC, 45 F.4th 1004, 1017 (D.C. Cir. 2022). 
18 Illinois Commerce Comm’n v. FERC, 576 F.3d 470, 477 (7th Cir. 2009). 
19 BNP Paribas Energy Trading GP v. FERC, 743 F.3d 264, 268 (D.C. Cir. 2014).  
20 RBP Proposal at 25-26.  
21 Id., Attachment C, Croop Affidavit at P 5.  
22 RBP Proposal at 6-7.  
23 Id.

11 
 
PJM’s proposed RBP cost-allocation mechanism assigns costs only to those Electric Distribution 
zones where load growth is forecasted, as measured by load adjustments between 2026 and 
2028.24 This allocation is particularly problematic because it remains fixed for the entire 15-year 
RBP commitment term. If forecasted large load is delayed, reduced, canceled, or never 
materialized, the RBP obligation assigned based on that forecast could remain with the Electric 
Distributor and ultimately be borne by its remaining retail customers. PJM has not adequately 
explained how a fixed allocation continues to reflect cost causation when the load on which it 
was based materially changes or fails to materialize. 
 
A central flaw of this paradigm is that the shortfall’s cause is not solely large-load 
customer growth. Even PJM recognizes that “it is well-documented and recognized that supply 
and demand in the PJM Region have converged, as a significant portion of PJM’s thermal 
generation fleet have retired while replacement resources are arriving at a slower pace….”25 PJM 
acknowledges that: “Together, these factors have strained the RPM Auction’s ability to procure 
sufficient capacity to meet the PJM Region Reliability Requirement in recent capacity 
auctions.”26 Thus, as PJM itself explains, the shortfall in the capacity market arose not only from 
large-load growth but also from a reduction in supply and the inability to bring new generation 
online. 
 
Those retirements did not occur in a vacuum, nor did they occur suddenly. Many of them 
were precipitated by the policies of states whose Electric Distributors will not be bearing costs 
associated with the RBP as PJM has proposed it. The reduction in supply is a PJM-wide 
phenomenon that PJM had been warning stakeholders and the Commission about long before the 
 
24 RBP Proposal, Attachment C, Croop Affidavit at PP 41, 43.  
25 RBP Proposal at 28.  
26 Id. (emphasis added).

12 
 
unexpected surge in load growth. As early as PJM’s February 24, 2023, report Energy Transition 
in PJM: Resource Retirements, Replacements & Risks, PJM noted that significant amounts of 
generation had retired and was slated to retire.27 Between 2012 and 2022, 47.2 GW ICAP 
retired.28 Figure 1 of the 4R Report highlights that PJM was projecting 40 GW of retirements by 
2030, composed of “12 GW of announced retirements, 25 GW of potential policy-driven 
retirements and 3 GW of potential economic retirements. Combined, this represents 21% of 
PJM’s current installed capacity.”29 The Independent Market Monitor for PJM echoed those 
concerns in its 2023 State of the Market Report for PJM, commenting that “an estimated total of 
between 24,000 MW and 58,000 MW of thermal resources are at risk of retirement, including 
4,285 MW of announced retirements, 19,635 MW of retirements as a result of state and federal 
environmental regulations, and 33,744 MW of retirements for economic reasons, based on 
expected forward prices.”30 So PJM’s recognition 1,294.4 MW ICAP added between the 
2027/2028 and 2028/2029 BRA fails to also recognize the removal of 47,200 MW ICAP over a 
little more than the past decade. 
 
The renewables that replaced the retiring thermal generation could replace the energy, but 
not the capacity, and the interconnection queue could not proceed efficiently enough to bring 
new generation online.31 The shortfall is, to a significant degree, as much the product of state 
policy choices as it is large-load growth. As Commissioner Christie articulated in the 
transmission context: 
 
27 Energy Transition in PJM: Resource Retirements, Replacements & Risks at 6-7 (dated Feb. 24, 2023) (Available 
at: https://www.pjm.com/-/media/DotCom/library/reports-notices/special-reports/2023/energy-transition-in-pjm-
resource-retirements-replacements-and-risks.ashx) (“4R Report”). 
28 Id. at 6.  
29 Id. at 5 (internal citations omitted). 
30 IMM, 2023 State of the Market Report for PJM Volume I at 1 (March 14, 2024) 
(https://www.monitoringanalytics.com/reports/pjm_state_of_the_market/2023.shtml) (“2023 State of the Market”). 
31 Id. at 2.

13 
 
Let me emphasize that the State of Maryland, within its sovereign police 
powers, clearly has the authority to mandate any particular mix of 
generating resources it prefers. Maryland's new climate law is well within 
its inherent authority to enact. Such policies are for Marylanders to choose, 
not RTOs or FERC. But if the resulting transmission projects under protest 
in this RTEP filing are caused more by Maryland's policy choices than by 
organic load growth and economic resource retirements, then a salient 
question that may be asked is whether these transmission projects are more 
accurately categorized as public policy projects, essentially the same as the 
transmission upgrades caused by New Jersey's offshore wind projects? 
 
And if they are more accurately categorized as public policy projects, 
should such projects be regionally cost-allocated, potentially to consumers 
in Pennsylvania, West Virginia, Ohio, et al.? For example, the State of 
Illinois has a law similar to Maryland's that PJM has already estimated will 
cause $2 billion in transmission upgrades, costs that will be allocated to 
consumers in other states under PJM's existing cost-allocation formula.32 
 
It is an equally salient question as to how the RBP is just and reasonable when it attributes, 
contrary to even PJM’s admission, all the costs associated with the shortfall to large-load growth 
during a PJM-wide phenomenon of supply constriction. 
 
The RBP is not just and reasonable because it does not match cost and causation. Large-
load growth is a cause, certainly, but not the only cause. The truth is that causation also is 
attributable to the diffuse effect of state environmental policies and the interconnection queue. 
The fact that the problem ballooned to this extent is because of the fundamental dysfunction of 
the PJM RPM, which has been unable to respond effectively to either an increase in demand or a 
decrease in supply. Although characterized as a reaction to load growth, the RBP is, in reality, 
another iteration of the “perpetual tweaking”33 needed to keep the PJM RPM wheezing along, in 
the same tradition as the Minimum Offer Price Rule34 and the price collar.35 
 
32 PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 185 FERC ¶ 61,107, PP 7-8 (2023) (Christie, Comm’r, concurring). 
33 Mark C. Christie, It’s Time to Reconsider Single-Clearing Price Mechanisms in U.S. Energy Markets, 44 Energy 
L.J. 1, 26 (2023).  
34 Calpine Corp. v. PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 163 FERC ¶ 61,236 (2018). 
35 PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 191 FERC ¶ 61,066 (2025).

14 
 
 
PJM has acknowledged that the RPM is ill-suited for it purpose, and indeed has not 
allowed the RPM to work as it’s designed. Rather than allow the RPM to clear at a price 
intended to spur the entry of new generation, PJM entered a settlement agreement to “cap [] 
power plant capacity prices.”36 Mr. Mosier is correct that suppressing the market signals to enter 
the market undermines investor confidence in the markets – “credibility trap” is PJM’s phrase for 
it.37 There is also likely merit to his assertion that “the ability to obtain 15-year price certainty in 
a backstop procurement likely chilled new entry in PJM’s most recent capacity auction.”38 
NOVEC should also point out that there is a mechanism in the PJM RPM -- the Reliability 
Backstop Auction -- specifically to address consecutive capacity shortfalls which PJM is also 
preempting in favor of yet another temporary “fix.”39 
 
If NOVEC (or others) cannot assign these costs directly to large loads, then the results 
should be viewed through the lens of whether the actual cost allocation is just and reasonable, 
and not whether a hypothetical allocation occurred. Viewed through that lens, the proposal does 
not satisfy the cost-causation principle because it does not match even one iota of the burden of 
the shortfall to the rest of PJM, notwithstanding the policy-driven retirements of generation that 
contributed to the shortfall. Unless the Commission revises the effective date or PJM voluntarily 
agrees to, the Commission should reject the RBP as a violation of the cost-causation principle. 
 
36 EKPC Letter at 2.  
37 PJM, Powering Reliability Through Market Design: Addressing Rising Demand and Constrained Supply, and 
Stimulating Investment to Support Durable Reliability at 5-6 (May 6, 2026) (https://www.pjm.com/-
/media/DotCom/library/reports-notices/special-reports/2026/20260506-powering-reliability-through-market-
design.pdf).  
38 EKPC Letter at 2.  
39 RBP Proposal at 123-125.

15 
 
C. 
The RBP improperly concentrates the incremental costs of RBP Resources on RBP 
buyers while allowing the resulting capacity-market benefits to accrue more 
broadly. 
PJM’s proposed RBP framework does not adequately account for the market-wide benefits 
that RBP Resources may provide. RBP buyers would bear the incremental RBP Charges and 
associated credit obligations attributable to the RBP Resources allocated to them. Yet those 
resources would participate in the same RPM Auctions that establish capacity prices paid by load 
throughout the relevant capacity market. To the extent RBP Resources increase available supply 
and reduce RPM clearing prices, those benefits are not confined to the LSEs assigned RBP cost 
responsibility. They accrue to other capacity purchasers as well. 
The RBP framework requires RBP Resources to offer their committed capacity into the 
RPM Auctions as price takers at $0. PJM explains that this requirement is appropriate because the 
RBP Resources are already being paid for by the responsible LSEs and because it ensures that an 
RBP Resource clears the RPM Auction, thereby avoiding the potential for load to pay twice for 
the same capacity. NOVEC does not dispute the objective of preventing duplicative payment 
obligations, but PJM’s solution has an important cost-allocation consequence that its proposal does 
not adequately address requiring RBP-supported capacity to offer at $0 can affect RPM clearing 
outcomes for market participants that bear no corresponding share of the incremental RBP costs. 
The significance of that requirement follows from the operation of RPM. Adding RBP 
Resources at a mandatory $0 offer increases the quantity of capacity offered at the bottom of the 
supply curve. Depending on market conditions, locational constraints, and the position of the 
marginal resource, those offers can reduce the RPM clearing price that otherwise would have 
resulted. Where that occurs, the resulting reduction in capacity prices benefits capacity purchasers 
generally, not merely the RBP buyers that financially support the RBP Resources.

16 
 
The incremental financial obligations associated with those resources, however, remain 
concentrated on the LSEs assigned RBP cost responsibility. Those LSEs must fund applicable 
RBP Charges and support those obligations through PJM’s proposed collateral requirements, while 
other market participants may receive lower capacity prices resulting from the same resources 
without bearing a corresponding share of those incremental costs. 
The RBP’s contract-for-differences settlement structure compounds this mismatch. RBP 
Resources receive RPM revenues that offset their RBP commitment payments. If the mandatory 
$0 offers of RBP Resources contribute to a lower RPM clearing price, those resources receive less 
RPM revenue and the corresponding RBP settlement obligation increases. RBP buyers therefore 
may bear a larger RBP Charge at the same time that the lower RPM price produces savings for 
capacity purchasers more broadly. In that circumstance, the same market effect that benefits non-
RBP buyers increases the incremental obligation imposed on RBP buyers. 
This allocation raises concerns under the Commission’s cost-causation principles. 
Although cost allocation need not correspond precisely to benefits received, the Commission has 
required costs to bear a reasonable relationship to the burdens imposed and benefits received and 
has recognized that substantial departures from that principle can create inappropriate cross-
subsidization. PJM has not adequately demonstrated why the incremental costs and substantial 
credit obligations associated with RBP Resources should be concentrated on designated RBP 
buyers without accounting for material capacity-market benefits those resources may provide to 
other PJM load. 
At a minimum, the Commission should require PJM to demonstrate that its proposed 
allocation of RBP costs is roughly commensurate with the benefits attributable to the RBP 
Resources. If PJM’s mandatory $0 offer requirement produces material market-wide capacity-

17 
 
price benefits, PJM should explain why those benefits do not warrant broader allocation of at least 
some portion of the incremental RBP costs or another mechanism that recognizes the value 
received by non-RBP buyers. 
The potential effect of such offers on RPM clearing prices is not merely theoretical. In 
considering the operation of PJM’s capacity market in another context, the Third Circuit 
recognized that artificially low capacity offers can “crowd out other capacity that is priced at a 
higher, cost-based rate” and thereby produce a lower clearing price.40 NOVEC does not contend 
that RBP Resources are similarly situated to the state-supported resources at issue in New Jersey 
BPU. The relevant point is narrower: PJM’s requirement that RBP Resources offer at $0 can affect 
the RPM clearing price, and any resulting price reduction benefits capacity purchasers beyond the 
LSEs required to bear the incremental costs of supporting those resources. 
D. 
The RBP framework is not just and reasonable because it requires too many MW to 
offset the RBP Target and encourages free riding.  
 
The RBP framework is unjust and unreasonable because the Qualifying RBP Offset 
UCAP MW to offset each Electric Distributor’s zone is too high relative to their pro rata share 
of the Initial RBP Target. The initial allocation of the RBP UCAP MW is based on each Electric 
Distributor’s zone’s share of the Initial RBP Target of 6,831.3 MW.41 NOVEC, for example, is 
assigned 1,302.6 MW.42 Even though NOVEC’s “share” of the shortfall is 1,302.6 MW, PJM’s 
proposal would require NOVEC to procure approximately 1,619 MW to fully offset 1,302.6 
MW.43 If the Initial RBP Target of 6,831.3 MW is the goal to offset, it is unjust and unreasonable 
to force RBP buyers to procure an excess of that target MW amount. The excess MW provide

(0.9401). This is representative of the self-supply obligation.”).

18 
 
additional value to the PJM capacity market for which the RBP buyer is not compensated. 
Similarly, the RBP reduces other buyers’ obligations when a single buyer procures Qualifying 
RBP Offset UCAP MW, which creates a perverse incentive for buyers willing to risk assignment 
of the RBP Charges to do nothing with the hope that other RBP buyers enter bilateral 
arrangements and reduce the Final RBP Target.  
E. 
The RBP is not just and reasonable because it relies on load forecasts that were 
prepared without knowledge or consideration of PJM’s newly proposed RBP 
paradigm. 
 
The RBP is intended to address the shortfall that occurred in the 2028/2029 BRA, but it 
assigns responsibility to that shortfall using the load adjustments from 2026 to 2028 submitted by 
LSEs. NOVEC has reservations about the use of the load adjustments “to ultimately determine 
the initial allocated pro-rata share to each relevant Electric Distributor zone/area.”44 PJM has not 
explained why this snapshot in time is appropriate beyond references to Schedule 8 of the RAA, 
which does not suffice.45 The load adjustments set forth in PJM Table B9b from the 2026 PJM 
Load Forecast are something of a black box.46  
 
The problem with relying on the load adjustments is, even if they are “firm,” all the load 
indicated interest based on economic circumstances that no longer exist.47 The RBP will raise 
costs of data center loads, which will either prompt marginal data center projects to withdraw or 
cause data centers to relocate to areas that are not assessed RBP Charges so that they can avoid 
these additional costs. If loads had known about the RBP, their plans would be different, they

materializes. In order to account for this effect, the Commission should either reject the filing or 
reduce the amount of RBP MWs that are allocated to NOVEC and other RBP buyers.  
F. 
The RBP’s collateral requirements on RBP buyers are unjust and unreasonable 
because it is unduly burdensome, excessive, and has not been shown to be necessary. 
 
PJM “is proposing to require that those LSEs allocated RBP cost responsibility for a 
given Delivery Year must post credit associated with such obligation.”48 PJM argues that this 
credit obligation is just and reasonable because “it is designed [to prevent] those LSEs not 
allocated cost responsibility for RBP Resources from having to pay for such resources” 
notwithstanding the benefit those LSEs derive from the new generation themselves.49 The RBP 
credit requirement “is a function of two inputs: the RBP Credit Rate and RBP UCAP MW 
committed.”50 The RBP UCAP MW input is the total amount of RBP UCAP MW committed 
through the RBP, as adjusted for resources that do not come online.51 
 
PJM is proposing to set the RBP Credit Rate at $1.5 million per MW initially, but it can 
be reduced to reflect a reduction in the total RBP UCAP MW or when total posted RBP 
Collateral exceeds the total RBP Charges obligation.52 PJM states that it set the credit rate at $1.5 
million based on an estimate of “the contractual value associated with a 1-MW RBP commitment 
using conservative assumptions, including a 15-year commitment term application of the RBP 
price throughout that commitment period.”53 Assuming the RBP clearing price is at the price cap 
of $555/MW-day, PJM estimated the contractual value of a 1-MW RBP commitment at $3.04

million.54 PJM then reduced the $3.04 million to $1.5 million so that PJM would hold “sufficient 
collateral to cover approximately 50% of the notional value of all RBP commitments….”55 
 
As set forth in Mr. Rollins’ affidavit, NOVEC estimates that its collateral requirement 
under PJM’s proposed regime would be approximately $1.95 billion.56 The collateral 
requirement is an extraordinary imposition on NOVEC. Indeed, the collateral requirement 
exceeds NOVEC’s total assets.57 NOVEC is uncertain whether it would even be able to secure 
$2 billion in collateral.58 As Mr. Rollins explains, the collateral requirement will disrupt 
NOVEC’s ordinary business operations.59 The Commission should not approve a collateral 
requirement that is an impossibility, a hindrance to an entity’s ability to operate, and an injustice. 
 
The need to reject or modify the collateral obligation is heightened by the calculation’s 
obvious defects. PJM “conservatively” requires the collateral obligation of the buyers to span the 
entire 15-year period.60 This expansive requirement simply is not necessary, as the risk could be 
significantly mitigated by a shorter period, such as three years. As Mr. Rollins discusses, the 
most significant obstacle to NOVEC fulfilling its RBP obligations is, ironically, the size of the 
RBP collateral obligation itself and not the RBP Charges.61 Indeed, PJM does not believe that a 
15-year collateral obligation on sellers is appropriate, noting that it limited the sellers’ collateral 
obligation to three years to avoid making the collateral requirement “onerous.”62 NOVEC does 
not see why it is just and reasonable for buyers to suffer under what even PJM deems an

Ms. Kelly states in her affidavit for PJM that the collateral requirement assumes that the

an “application of a simple formula based on the RBP Charge obligation over 15 years, i.e., the

are providing collateral to ensure that everyone in PJM pays the capacity costs associated with 
the RBP Resources. RBP buyers themselves already provide PJM collateral to ensure that they 
pay their capacity rates under Attachment Q, and so do all other capacity buyers.67 PJM is

It is unnecessary to require that 50% of the total payments be held as collateral. Although 
PJM contends that this provides “commensurate” protection against non-payment,69 NOVEC has 
demonstrated that the actual RBP Charges will be less than $555/MW-day. The total amount 
held as collateral could exceed the ultimate payments made by the RBP buyers.70 The collateral 
amount should not exceed a level that is commensurate with actual RBP obligations. PJM asserts 
that to test the reasonableness of the $1.5 million per MW figure, PJM used a 9.5% discount rate 
developed by consultants from The Brattle Group based on the average weighted cost of capital 
for participants in the RPM.71 PJM’s reliance on calculations from a Brattle report does not 
substantiate PJM’s assertion that its figure is just and reasonable. For one, it was developed for 
another purpose and does not necessarily translate to a risk of non-payment. The figure is 
designed for ordinary generators, not generators who will have a guaranteed revenue stream for 
15 years. Those generators face much lower risk and do not need as high a return. 
 
The Tariff is ambiguous as to when the collateral obligation will be reduced and does not 
appear to properly reduce it over time. Ms. Kelly states that “PJM concluded that the remaining 
payment exposure naturally declines as remaining, forward RBP payment obligations are 
satisfied and as committed RBP Resources are removed from the portfolio through rescinded

total existing RBP Charges obligations….”74 It is not just and reasonable to grant PJM the 
discretion to determine whether RBP buyers should be required to post more collateral than the 
total existing RBP Charges obligations, especially given that their calculation already overstates 
the likely RBP Charges.  
 
The circumstances in which the collateral obligation is reduced are too few. The RBP 
Credit Rate should be reduced to account for the remaining term over which RBP Charges will 
be paid. If 50% of the total RBP Charges is the standard (and it should be lower for the reasons 
discussed in prior paragraphs), then it should be 50% or less of the remaining RBP Charges in 
each year. If PJM believes that 50% of the total payment obligations at the start of the 15-year 
term is sufficient, then the same percentage of the total remaining payment obligations should be 
the cap for each year.  
 
If the Commission does not reject the filing, then it should require revisions on 
compliance to reduce the collateral obligation so that it corresponds to the actual risk imposed on

PJM’s markets. The Commission should require PJM to allow other methods to demonstrate 
creditworthiness besides posting the full collateral or a letter of credit. NOVEC maintains an 
investment-grade credit rating and has met its obligations to PJM. Given NOVEC’s investment-
grade credit rating, financial condition, and established record of satisfying its PJM obligations, 
PJM should permit NOVEC to satisfy all or a substantial portion of the requirement through 
unsecured credit or another demonstration of creditworthiness rather than requiring cash 
collateral or a letter of credit for the full notional amount. If the Commission does not allow 
alternative demonstrations of creditworthiness, the Commission should correct PJM’s defective 
collateral calculations. The Commission should require the collateral calculation to reflect the 
actual clearing price of the RBP auction. Instead of providing for an “onerous” 15-year term, the 
Commission should limit the period collateralized to three years, just as PJM proposes to do for 
generators. Additionally, the Commission should also limit the collateral amount to the expected 
incremental amount between the RBP clearing price and the expected capacity-market revenue to 
avoid duplicative collateral requirements. 
III. 
STAKEHOLDER PROCESS 
 
Rather than attempt to salvage the RBP Proposal, the Commission should exercise its 
authority under NRG to implement the voluntary subscription model the stakeholders approved 
as part of the CIFP process. PJM’s CIFP process is intended to expedite resolution of issues 
critical to PJM. As such, while decisions from it are ultimately the Board’s to make, PJM 
members and other stakeholders play a key advisory role by signaling solutions they agree with 
through a four-stage proposal-development and voting process. Indeed, members have been 
criticized in past iterations of the CIFP for not coming to clear consensus. Members sent the 
Board a clear message in this CIFP by supporting one proposal from more than a dozen

25 
 
considered. That proposal included an interconnected package of reforms that were carefully 
balanced to address the issue while maintaining mitigation options for LSEs, all headlined by a 
version of the RBP auction that would have required LSEs to “subscribe” to obligations, i.e. they 
had control to mitigate their forecasted growth by committing to curtail it instead of accepting a 
capacity obligation and resulting costs. NOVEC supported that proposal and still does. 
 
The Board clearly appreciated members’ message by adopting portions of the proposal 
that it found favorable but rejecting those it did not, including the key tool for LSEs to mitigate 
their potential obligations in the auction: the subscription-based auction. By pulling out that 
component of the proposal, PJM effectively stripped LSEs of their control over accepting RBP 
obligations. In NOVEC’s view, that control was critical to the success of the RBP process, which 
should embody a bottom-up, rather than a top-down approach. The bottom-up process gives truly 
interested developers the option to subscribe to pay the RBP costs rather than accept an 
interruptible form of service which PJM has proposed in Docket No. ER26-3515 (the Interim 
Resource Adequacy Service or “IRAS”). Contrary to the PJM Board’s determination, the 
voluntary subscription framework would provide sufficient assurance that capacity equal to the 
identified near-term shortfall would actually be procured.75 Paired with IRAS, committed load is 
adequately incentivized to participate to avoid an interruptible service—their business models 
rely on reliable service. 
 
Although NOVEC rejects the premise that the voluntary subscription process would fail, 
even if it procured less than the total shortfall, that should not be considered a failure when 
considered in the context of the package of reforms the stakeholders proposed. The IRAS 
effectively mitigates any reliability harm, and if load prefers to avoid IRAS through bringing its 
 
75 RBP Proposal at 21.

26 
 
own generation rather than participating in the RBP, it makes sense to allow that option. Either 
way, PJM obtains the generation it needs, and the large load is better situated to make that 
determination. More to the point, the subscription process avoids many of the issues discussed 
above because it allows LSEs to make arrangements directly with willing participants. FERC 
should order PJM to revise its RBP auction structure to be subscription-based with the load 
growth that is not subscribed being subject to curtailment by default, as contemplated by the 
stakeholder proposal. 
IV. 
CONCLUSION 
WHEREFORE, for the foregoing reasons, NOVEC respectfully requests that the 
Commission reject the RBP Filing. If the Commission does not reject the filing, it should accept 
PJM’s invitation76 to require changes to the RBP to rectify the mistakes discussed above, 
including extending the effective date to allow for the RBP to have a chance of success, revising 
the cost-allocation structure to recognize the benefits derived from RBP Resources by non-RBP 
buyers, adjusting the amount of MW needed to offset RBP cost responsibility, shifting the 
auction to a subscription-based model, and reducing the collateral requirements as discussed 
above. At a minimum, the Commission should issue a deficiency letter and require PJM to better 
explain both its rejection of the coalition proposal and the as-filed RBP’s design.
